::: {.callout-important}
## Read this before you start

Section A is the big one, because Q20 is the question to master. Re-read the clinic's two concept boxes
before you start it — **the feedback is a number, not a yes or no**, and **"guarantee" means worst case**.

Throughout Section A, the password is a rearrangement of the five letters $a,b,c,d,e$, every guess is also a
rearrangement of those five letters, and the computer replies with **how many letters are in the correct
position**.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** "How many attempts" → a whole number, with a reason why fewer will not do. Candidate lists →
every candidate written out. Ranges → an inequality with each endpoint stated as included or excluded.
Orderings → a value of $x$ that works, or a proof that none does.

**Total: 48 marks.**
:::

# Section A — Deduction

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[5 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
I enter **abcde** and am told that none of the letters are in the correct position. I enter **bcdea** and am
told the same.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Build the grid of letters still allowed in each position.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** How many candidates remain?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Using the best strategy, how many **further** attempts are needed to guarantee the
password? Justify why fewer will not do.
:::

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[5 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Suppose three guesses all return $0$, and suppose further that the three guesses **differ from one another in
every position**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Explain why every position then has exactly two allowed letters, and why every letter is
allowed in exactly two positions.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Hence explain why the number of candidates can never be exactly **one** — so that
"**None: I can deduce it immediately**" is never the right answer to a question of this shape.

*Hint for (b): draw the five positions and the five letters as two rows of dots, joining each position to the
two letters it allows. What shape must that picture be?*
:::

::: {.question}

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Exactly three of the six can occur. Say which, giving a value of $x$ for each.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Prove that the other three can never occur. *One short inequality kills all three at
once.*

# Section C — The four speed drills

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
$y=a^{x}$ is drawn with a solid line, where $a>1$. A second curve $y=f(x)$ is drawn dashed; it passes through
the same point on the $y$-axis but rises **less** steeply. Which of these could be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** $f(x)=b^{x}$ for some $b>a$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **2** $f(x)=b^{x}$ for some $b<a$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** $f(x)=a^{kx}$ for some $k>1$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **4** $f(x)=a^{kx}$ for some $k<1$

State which, and give the one-line rewrite that makes it obvious.
:::

Working
:::

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
$f(x)$ is defined for all real $x$. Which one of the following is a **sufficient** condition for
$\displaystyle\int_3^7 f(x)\,\mathrm dx=0$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(5)=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $f(3)=f(7)=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x+5)=-f(5-x)$ for all $x$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $f(x-5)=-f(5-x)$ for all $x$

Give a counterexample for each of the four that fail.
:::

Working
:::

## Before you hand it in

- [ ] I justified why a smaller number of attempts will **not** do, not only that my number works.
- [ ] Where I claimed an ordering is impossible, I proved it; where I claimed one is possible, I gave an $x$.

- [ ] For the "must be true" question I gave a counterexample for each statement I rejected.
